summary:
Same-sex conduct is not criminalised in Vietnam. The 2015 Civil Code, Article 37, recognised transgender people's right to change their legal gender, and a November 2015 milestone allowed people who had changed gender to apply for a civil-status change. The implementing legislation has not followed. A draft law protecting transgender people's legal status was expected to be discussed by the National Assembly with completion targeted for 2020, and a recognition draft law was still under consideration as of February 2026. The right to legal gender recognition therefore exists in statute without an operative procedure.

No law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, according to Freedom House as cited by the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada. Amnesty International's 2025 report finds that LGBTI people's rights lack meaningful protection in both law and practice.

Same-sex marriage was removed from the list of forbidden acts in 2015, but the unions it permits confer no legal rights and are not registered by the state.

Public space for LGBTI organising narrowed during 2025. Ho Chi Minh City abruptly cancelled its flagship Pride march, and at least five other Pride events were cancelled that year. Human Rights Watch Asia director Patricia Gossman described the cancellations as worrying signs of a government clampdown on LGBTQ+ rights, against Vietnam's long-standing reputation for tolerance toward sexual minorities.

Healthcare access is impeded by administration rather than by provider hostility in many accounts. Transgender women report routine discrimination at healthcare encounters, including staff asking why their appearance does not match their identity documents, alongside heightened scrutiny. Four trans Vietnamese patients described respectful providers whose care was undone by administrative red tape. The Ministry of Health declared in August 2022 that same-sex attraction and transgender identity are not mental disorders.

Trans women face economic- and stigma-driven risk of physical and sexual violence, reported most acutely for trans women in northern provinces and ethnic-minority communities. No trans-specific killing has been documented here.

Conversion efforts (SOGICE) are documented in the Vietnamese context. A Lighthouse Vietnam study published in October 2024 set out the lived experiences and forms of SOGICE among LGBTIQ people and identified data needs.

Detention carries a specific unresolved risk. In January 2015 the Social, Economic and Environmental Institute proposed to the Ministry of Public Security that homosexual and transgender prisoners be housed separately from the general prison population to protect them from sexual harassment, citing a 2014 survey in which most transgender prisoners wanted separate jails. It stated that existing prison infrastructure allowed transgender prisoners to be held only in solitary confinement or mixed with the general population, with no housing wing matched to a prisoner's gender identity, and asked that prisoners be permitted to determine their own gender identity. No enacted outcome has been documented.

Wider repression forms the backdrop. Vague Penal Code articles 109, 116, 117 and 331 were used to arrest at least 43 people in 2025, and proposed press-law rules would require disclosure of sources. Vietnam was re-elected to the UN Human Rights Council for a term running to 2028.

For a visitor: no criminalisation, no trans-specific border friction documented, and unrestricted bathroom access, but no practical route to legal gender recognition and no statutory protection against discrimination.
tangentialFactors:
Vietnam's reputation for tolerance toward sexual minorities is the frame against which the 2025 Pride cancellations were read as a clampdown, so the direction of travel is the salient question rather than any single prohibition.

LGBTIQ organisations operate openly in Vietnam, which distinguishes the environment from jurisdictions where such groups are banned, but they do so under government surveillance.

The absence of legal gender recognition is the mechanism behind most downstream friction: identity documents that do not match presentation drive healthcare scrutiny, administrative delay and heightened exposure to violence.

The country's re-election to the UN Human Rights Council until 2028 sits alongside Amnesty International's findings on vague criminal provisions and arrests, indicating that LGBTI-specific concerns form part of a broader civic-space pattern rather than an isolated file.

No law prohibits non-consensual intersex medical interventions, an adjacent gap in the same legal framework.
localsOnly:
Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination in education, employment, housing or healthcare on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity; the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada's multi-source briefing on Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City documents how this plays out across those settings.

Legal gender recognition remains unavailable in practice despite Article 37 of the 2015 Civil Code, so residents must rely on documents that do not reflect their gender, with the administrative consequences that follow.

The Ministry of Health's August 2022 declaration that same-sex attraction and transgender identity are not mental disorders is the operative official position for residents seeking care.

Same-sex couples may marry but acquire no rights from doing so, and LGBTIQ organisations may register and operate openly subject to state surveillance.

Prisoners who are transgender or gay have no housing arrangement matched to their gender identity, and the 2015 proposal to create separate accommodation has no documented enacted outcome.

Conversion efforts are documented as a lived experience among LGBTIQ people, with no statutory prohibition on the practice.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the recognition draft law under consideration as of February 2026 has since been passed is unresolved in the sources; the most recent dated evidence places it still before the legislature.

The 2015 prison-housing proposal has no documented enacted outcome, and no source confirms whether any subsequent policy on the placement of transgender prisoners was adopted.

No source in the inventory records a trans-specific killing in Vietnam, and the absence of such a record is not the same as a verified zero.

Whether the 2025 Pride cancellations were a single-year decision or a continuing policy is unresolved; the evidence covers 2025 events only.

The inventory does not state whether Vietnam imposes any entry, visa or border screening that turns on gender markers or presentation, so no finding is offered on that point.
